clue.text: Ready for Spring? Jessop may perhaps occur to her

indicators.note: 'may perhaps' suggests the following letters could be rearranged into something else

parts.note: the word 'to' only links; 'her' is taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzle about who is poised to leap in spring, and whether a famous cricketer might come to mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert Jessop, an English batsman of around 1900, was nicknamed 'The Croucher' for his low stance; anyone poised to spring crouches. 'may perhaps' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ready to leap is crouched low, and the cricketer Jessop's famous nickname described his stooping stance.

clue.text: Little room for 3-D French article

parts.note: three-dimensional is cubic, having volume
le is the French masculine definite article

explanation.surface: A small room fitted out for a stereoscopic French feature.
explanation.definitionFit: A cubicle is a small partitioned compartment, as in a changing booth.

clue.text: What many do to few-the toll of wickets down

explanation.surface: A cricketing remark on a heavy loss of wickets, echoing Churchill's 'the many' and 'the few'.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is OUT NUMBER: the count of batsmen who are out.
explanation.definitionFit: A larger group exceeds a smaller one in count; and in cricket, the tally of dismissed batsmen is literally the number out.

clue.text: Spenser's "well of English undefiled"

parts.note: Edmund Spenser, in The Faerie Queene, praised the earlier poet of The Canterbury Tales with this phrase

explanation.surface: A literary quotation about pure English prose springing from a source.
explanation.definitionFit: The Faerie Queene's author honoured the Canterbury Tales poet as the pure fountain of the English tongue.

clue.text: Digs up about a thousand colours? Say ten first

indicators.note: 'first' puts the spoken letter at the front of what follows
'Say' asks for the name of the letter as spoken rather than written

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral ten

indicators.note: 'about' has the colours word going around the thousand

parts.note: hues are colours
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: An excavator wonders about a vast range of colours and counting to ten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say ten' means pronounce the Roman numeral as a letter name; 'about' wraps the colours round the thousand, and 'first' puts the spoken letter in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhume is to dig a buried body out of the ground.

clue.text: One's home in England?

parts.note: refers to the saying that an Englishman's home is his fortified residence

explanation.surface: A question about where a person lives in England.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'an Englishman's home is his castle' says every householder is lord of his own place.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortified residence of a lord, as the English proverb grants to every householder.

clue.text: He stands to suit

parts.note: read as someone who stands for election to take a seat in Parliament

explanation.surface: A tailor's client standing to be fitted for a suit.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'sit' (OCR gave 'suit'): one who stands for election hopes to sit in Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: A person seeking election 'stands' for office, hoping to sit as a member.

clue.text: Writing bill, artists raised bitter taunts

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the whole run is read from bottom to top

parts.note: MS is short for manuscript, a piece of writing
AC is short for account, a bill
RAs are Royal Academicians, artists

explanation.surface: Artists protesting at a bill they were charged for their writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns MS + AC + RAS upwards, giving SARCASM.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocking, cutting remarks meant to wound are irony used as a weapon.

clue.text: Out of time yet in order for baby

indicators.note: 'in' places one word inside the other

parts.note: late means out of time, overdue

explanation.surface: A tardy, muddled order placed for an infant.
explanation.definitionFit: A full set of clothing and bedding prepared for a newborn is ordered as one outfit.

clue.text: Mad baronet takes a Greek islander for a frog

indicators.note: 'Mad' says the baronet abbreviation is jumbled

parts.note: Bart is the abbreviation of baronet
a Chian is a native of the Greek island of Chios

explanation.surface: A crazed aristocrat mistakes a man from a Greek island for a frog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' rearranges BART to BATR; 'takes' adds A and CHIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Batrachian is the zoological word for frogs and toads, the tailless amphibians.

clue.text: In Flint; both sides include Henry

indicators.note: 'include' has the two sides holding the name

parts.note: R and L are right and left, both sides
Hy is a standard abbreviation of Henry

explanation.surface: A remark that in a piece of flint, Henry appears on both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: Flint (Flintshire) is a Welsh county; Rhyl is a seaside town in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyl is a resort town located in the Welsh county of Flintshire.

clue.text: Christian Soldiers

parts.note: recalls the hymn 'Onward, Christian Soldiers' and the body of believers struggling on earth

explanation.surface: The hymn title 'Onward, Christian Soldiers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Theology's term for the faithful on earth who fight against sin, as soldiers of Christ.

clue.text: Note. Bond's boss impersonates dog, gets aboard.

parts.note: E is a musical note
M is James Bond's chief in the novels
barks is what one does to imitate a dog

explanation.surface: Bond's chief does a dog impression before boarding.
explanation.definitionFit: To embark is to go on board a ship or plane.

clue.text: Arch mason's concerns, or piano tuner's?

explanation.surface: Comparing what worries a builder of arches with what worries a piano tuner.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits as KEY'S TONES: the notes of a piano key.
explanation.definitionFit: Central wedge stones that lock an arch matter to a mason; the pitches of each key matter to a tuner.

clue.text: From Simon's store, was too much for Clarence

definitions.text: From Simon's store, was too much for Clarence

parts.words: From Simon's store, was too much for Clarence
parts.note: Simon the Cellarer's song tells of his store of this sweet wine; Shakespeare's Duke of Clarence was drowned in a butt of it

explanation.surface: Something from Simon's shop that overwhelmed a man called Clarence.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'it was too much'. In Richard III, the Duke of Clarence is drowned in a butt (cask) of this wine; 'Simon the Cellarer' is a Victorian song about a wine-keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet Madeira wine, kept by Simon the Cellarer in the song, and the cask wine that drowned Clarence.

clue.text: Mirror's Beauty Queen 14.

parts.note: the magic mirror in the fairy tale names the fairest of all, who outshines the wicked queen

explanation.surface: A tabloid's pin-up winner in a beauty contest.
explanation.walkthrough: The page has no '14.': OCR added it. 'Mirror' looks like the newspaper, but it is the fairy tale's magic mirror.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy-tale mirror declares this princess fairest in the land, so she is its beauty winner.

clue.text: Replays revised version of the truce talks

indicators.note: a revised version is the same letters reworked into a new form

explanation.surface: Replays offered as an amended account of negotiations for a ceasefire.
explanation.definitionFit: Parleys are discussions between enemies, typically to agree terms of a ceasefire.

clue.text: Brow-wringer alleviated by ministering angel

parts.note: quotes Scott's Marmion: 'When pain and ... wring the brow, A ministering angel thou!'

explanation.surface: A distress soothed by a kindly nurse figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Walter Scott's Marmion addresses woman: 'When pain and anguish wring the brow, A ministering angel thou!'
explanation.definitionFit: Severe mental suffering is what, in Scott's lines, wrings the brow until woman comforts it.

clue.text: Does Hell supply material for one's last work?

definitions.text: Does Hell supply material for one's last work?

parts.words: Does Hell supply material for one's last work?
parts.note: plays on the phrase 'hell for ...', and on a cobbler's last, the foot form on which shoes are made

explanation.surface: Asking whether the underworld inspires a writer's final work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last' looks like final, but it is the cobbler's foot-shaped block; the material for work on it is hide. 'Hell for leather' is an idiom for at full speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Tanned hide is the material a shoemaker works on the last, and it follows 'hell for' in the idiom.

clue.text: Answer-the engineer's water supply

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, so the engineer's gives RE'S
a pond is a body of water

explanation.surface: Replying to a question about the engineer's water source.
explanation.definitionFit: To reply to someone is to give them an answer.

clue.text: For him the tree in the quad exists, regardless

definitions.text: For him the tree in the quad exists, regardless

parts.words: For him the tree in the quad exists, regardless
parts.note: echoes the limerick on Berkeley's idealism about a tree in the quad that exists only when observed; this thinker holds it exists whether seen or not

explanation.surface: A philosopher's view about a tree in a college courtyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The limerick mocks Bishop Berkeley's idea that things exist only when perceived; the opposite camp believes objects exist independent of minds.
explanation.definitionFit: In philosophy, one who holds that physical objects exist independently of perception.

clue.text: Hold up as it might be in the sun

indicators.note: 'in' has the jumbled pair sit inside the sun

parts.note: sun taken as written, with 'the' as a pointer

indicators.note: 'might be' suggests the two words could be rearranged

explanation.surface: Wondering what it would be like to stay up in the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' is the anagram signal on 'as it', and 'in' places the result inside the sun; 'Hold up' means support, not delay.
explanation.definitionFit: To sustain is to support or bear the weight of something, keeping it up.

clue.text: In spite of which a wine may wet your whistle

definitions.text: In spite of which a wine may wet your whistle

parts.words: In spite of which a wine may wet your whistle
parts.note: a wine described as lacking sweetness still moistens the throat

explanation.surface: A remark on a wine that still quenches thirst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet your whistle' means have a drink; a wine can be called 'dry' yet still wet the throat.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of being not sweet in wine, or lacking moisture, which a drink paradoxically relieves.

clue.text: Soldier ants bring about a method of walking over water

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
to cause is to bring about
a way is a method

explanation.surface: Army ants creating a way of crossing water on foot.
explanation.walkthrough: The Giant's Causeway is a basalt rock formation on the Northern Irish coast; legend says the giant Finn McCool built it to walk to Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The basalt columns of County Antrim are, by legend, a giant's stepping road across the sea.

clue.text: Sweet girl ran away, to little dog's amusement

definitions.text: ran away, to little dog's amusement

explanation.surface: A girl ran off, and a small dog laughed.
explanation.walkthrough: From the nursery rhyme 'Hey Diddle Diddle': 'The little dog laughed to see such sport, And the dish ran away with the spoon.'
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for an attractive young woman; and the crockery that eloped with the spoon in the nursery rhyme.

clue.text: To me in vain the case is altered

indicators.note: 'is altered' says the letters before it are changed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A lawyer's frustration that a case has been changed without effect.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar, the subject case of nouns is one of the inflectional cases.

clue.text: Cat's-head Egyptian god that everybody sings

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: Horus is the falcon-headed Egyptian sky god

explanation.surface: An Egyptian deity with the head of a cat, celebrated in song.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a cat-headed god like Bastet; but 'Cat's-head' gives C, before HORUS.
explanation.definitionFit: The refrain of a song is the part all join in to sing.

clue.text: O.K. for looks, they're the opposite in effect

definitions.text: O.K. for looks, they're the opposite in effect

parts.words: O.K. for looks, they're the opposite in effect
parts.note: good-looking people are fine to look at, yet their effect is to knock you out, K.O. being O.K. backwards

explanation.surface: A comment that attractive people have an effect opposite to their looks.
explanation.walkthrough: To stun is to knock out (K.O.), the letters O.K. in the opposite order; beautiful people likewise leave you dazed.
explanation.definitionFit: Very attractive people are called knockouts because their beauty leaves admirers dazed.
